These 3D configurations were synthesized through a blend of optical motion capture (MoCap), FX technology, and actual functional hand movements. To address the challenge of accurately localizing small, often invisible rings within FX images using current standard ClrMoCap and other existing full-DoF pose recovery models, which typically depend on visual markers like rings or LEDs, our solution leverages the aforementioned DeepHMap framework. Specifically, we enhanced this pipeline by first applying a projection clustering approach and subsequently integrating an X-ray-to-3D surface correspondence module. This combination allows our proposed solution—deeply known as DeepHMap++—to successfully achieve full-DoF pose localization without the necessity of physical external objects. To validate our approach, extensive testing was conducted using the newly introduced FlexiHand dataset, alongside traditional Motion Capture datasets containing similar intricate movements. Additionally, deep comparisons were performed against leading pose recovery protocols to demonstrate superior performance through deepHMap++.

Although six of these structures remain controversial due to difficulties in experimentally verifying them, our data indicates they display exceptional stability across a broad spectrum of temperatures and pressures. Accurate pre-processing and quality control (QC) are essential for ensuring the reliability of clinical brain MRI analyses. Traditionally, QC workflows depend on manual inspections by experts or rule-based automatic systems; however, rule-based methods often fail due to the diverse and evolving nature of clinical MRI hardware, while rule-out cases indicate a significant need for fully automated solutions. In this study, we present a novel fully automatic QC framework that utilizes weak labels to flag rejects and distinguishes between cases of superior and average technical quality. Our contribution defines "brain MRI quality scoring" as a binary classification task—either flagging poor-quality images for rejection or differentiating high versus average quality images—sufficient to establish a robust framework for various clinical needs. We argue that applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to this binary classification utilizes available weak labels effectively to create a generalizable model. We assess this framework first using a multi-vendor multi-field strength dataset containing varying pathologies and technical characteristics, and second on two additional datasets featuring different rejection criteria and rejection rates. Our results demonstrate that weak-label MRI QC generalizes well to novel sites, new MRI scanners, and diverse pathologies. Furthermore, the MCMC approach appears more robust than standard supervised learning supervisory paradigms in these real-world clinical settings, highlighting the practical value of the proposed methodological strategy.

Addressing these challenges requires a dual focus: promoting staggered charging behaviors and developing robust grid architectures. This paper introduces a resilience-centric evaluation metric for electrical networks and presents a Multi-Agent Optimization (MAO) model designed to evaluate how privately owned EVs affect network resilience. Within this framework, a population of EV agents exhibits learning capabilities to choose optimal charging channels—either public or private—while a Power Utility Company (PUC) agent manages the system by optimizing the placement of charging stations. Private car owners minimize their total charging expenses, whereas the PUC seeks to optimize public infrastructure investment. Brownout occurrence and extent are modeled considering both physical network constraints and user behavior dynamics. Calibrated with a real 14,37-bus system in Taiwan, results indicate that evading the peak charge-demand window is critical, as failing to do so leads to blackouts even when stations are optimally sized and located.

This study analyzes a stochastic SIR (susceptible, infectious, recovered) epidemic model defined on a graph that evolves dynamically through a rewiring mechanism. This process alters the network's structure in response to an increase in infection levels. We establish the model's well-posedness and derive its mean-field approximation, investigating how it behaves when these elements scale large. Specifically, we prove that as the population grows to infinity, the trajectories of the proportion of infected and recovered individuals converge uniformly on a compact time interval to deterministic functions. Concurrently, the topological structure of the network converges to a limit characterized by a deterministic rewiring differential equation. We also approach the problem asymptotically with respect to the initial distribution of infections and provide insights into the dynamics of an initial epidemic wave, tracking how prevalence levels evolve. Furthermore, we examine how varying the initial network topology influences this wave behavior and describe the system's dependency on parameters, the peak infection prevalence, and the ultimate fraction of the population that becomes infected. The paper concludes by detailing the numerical strategies used for simulation.

In the domain of reinforcement learning within intricate, high-stakes activities like automatic driving, medical intelligence, robotic manipulation, and industrial arms, the complexity of acquiring extensive, diverse training data often presents a major hurdle. Variance reduction experience replay (VRER) serves as a suitable alternative by drawing upon a reservoir of prior knowledge, allowing algorithms to reach stable and efficient policy improvements despite limited new data. Nevertheless, due factors such as the variance inherent in bootstrapping and off-policy sampling VRER methods still contend with data imbalance and fluctuating performance policies. This study introduces a series of algorithm enhancements designed to further lower variance: Off-line Variance reduction Dynamics (OLVD), and two iterations named PVD-1 and PVD-2. OLVD refines data sampling strategies during offline training to variance weight sampling (VWS), while the subsequent PVD models extend these concepts to online environments, incorporating variance weighted sampling (VWS) for the target policy and importance sampling based bagging (ISB) for environment interaction respectively. Examinations across three benchmark online algorithms and three real-world applications demonstrate the superior efficacy of our proposed methods in achieving more robust learning outcomes compared to existing alternatives.

We introduce MultiTalk, a dialogue branching mechanism designed to dramatically expand the range of possible reply trajectories within dialogue systems evaluations, using existing benchmarks for real-world engagement, knowledge exchange, and small-talk. Current dialogue capability assessments largely depend on a few fixed, pre-established replies following an initial prompt; however, conversations become far more dynamic when responses branch based on prior content. While prior efforts have automated top-down expansion, they often yield repetitive or unnatural outcomes. Using a bottom-up strategy applied to real, high-fidelity dialogues from the XSTC and Facebook Benchmarks, MultiTalk automatically generates a detailed decision tree where each leaf represents a meticulously polished, contextually appropriate reply. We make this decision-tree structure, along with hundreds of new dialogue responses, publicly available. Empirical analyses comparing MultiTalk to standard benchmarks, plus visual comparisons of its generated outputs, highlight the framework's distinct advantages in creating more varied and authentic conversational experiences. Code and resources can be accessed here: https://multitalk.github.io/

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has established itself as a primary framework for advancing large language models (LLMs), though it remains constrained by a lack of task transferability. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge, has shown promising results on tasks distinct from those trained upon. This study introduces a new line of investigation into task transferability through either Knowledge Grounded Conversation (KGC) or, alternatively, RAG. Our findings reveal that models grounded in knowledge exhibit stronger generalization not only to other fact-based tasks, such as Question Answering, but also to creative writing prompts. Furthermore, these grounded models outperform non-grounded counterparts on these tasks, despite the non-transferable nature of question-answering itself. To enable generalization across a broader spectrum, including creative tasks, we proposed a specific form of retrieval-based dialogue known as Knowledge Grounded Conversation. Both empirical observations and our initial theoretical framework suggest that replacing the original dialogue with a form of "retrieved, knowledge-grounded conversation" can significantly boost the transferability of dialogue systems. We support this theory with extensive experiments, confirming the hypoized improvements in cross-task performance.

Optimizing hyperparameters represents a critical step in implementing and fine-tuning deep learning models, including privacy-preserving solutions. This addresses a significant challenge in real-world applications of differentialy private (DP) convolutional neural networks (CNNs), as adding noise to gradient updates disrupts the effectiveness of standard automated optimization techniques. Consequently, DP training often requires manual tuning by experts, which becomes particularly onerous as the architecture grows in complexity. While previous studies have examined parameter selection for specific DP model cases, investigations into hyperparameter optimization across broad classes of DP models have remained absent. In this work, we focus on FG-DP training, an adaptive optimizer tailored for DP stochastic gradient descent (SGDD). By conducting extensive experiments on three distinct model architectures—AlexNet, VGG-16, and ResNet-18 applied to image classification—we analyze the impact of key hyperparameters, specifically privacy parameters and batch sizes. Notably, we discover a previously unrecognized connection revealing that the optimal noise scale parameter is influenced by the training dataset's intrinsic variance rather than being arbitrary. Drawing on this insight, we propose HPFOG-DP, a novel method for DP hyperparameter optimization. HPFOG-DP automatically and efficiently calibrates remaining hyperparameters while selecting an optimal noise parameter with minimal additional classification variance, ensuring the process remains lightweight to preserve variance. Compared to current state-of-the-art methodologies, HPFOG-DP demonstrates superior performance in both automated optimization and variance noise reduction.

Planetary Nebulae (PNe) are formed via a mechanism involving the expulsion of stellar envelopes, occurring roughly 10 million to 1 billion years after formation. Flow processing involves executing one or more programs on a collection of data flows, which differ in granularity and scheduling—some items arrive continuously, while others are transmitted at specific intervals. As applications evolve to leverage high-bandwidth periodic streams capable carrying thousands of items per packet, traditional processing engines struggle to maintain efficiency. We introduce LifeStream, a novel network card-based platform designed for robust periodic streams. By exploiting temporal redundancy within these streams, LifeStream merges multiple flows into single, large payloads, achieving orders-of-magnitude performance gains over existing methods. This boost in throughput enables the deployment of more sophisticated and scalable processing technologies.

Smart wearables, although capable of monitoring various health indicators through sensors, often struggle with accurate wearable disease diagnosis due to limited professional knowledge. Traditional methods address this by training deep learning models on large, expert-curated datasets in a centralized cloud framework; however, such approaches conflict with strict data privacy requirements. Federated learning offers a decentralized alternative where training occurs locally on mobile devices and models are improved iteratively via server-based aggregation, thereby preserving privacy. Furthermore, prior work has utilized this technology to solve healthcare issues on other devices. In contrast, the challenging and diverse characteristics of different wearable models suggest a need for strategies beyond standard federation. Introducing the Wearable Healthcare Knowledge Transfer Framework (FedHealth), this framework operates on two pillars: first, it employs a fine-grained, layer-by-layer aggregation method to enhance existing hospital-grade models so they perform optimally on specific wearables; second, it implements a negative transfer mitigation strategy to ensure robust training accuracy across diverse wearable datasets. All data remains private on local devices throughout the process. Extensive experiments using real-world, high-dimensional physiological signals—covering eight types of wearables and involving over 2,000 participants—validate the effectiveness of our approach by demonstrating significant accuracy improvements across multiple disease identification tasks compared to current standards.

The rapid advancement in information technology fuelled a burst in news volume, yet this progress has concurrently triggered widespread misinformation and deceptive content. Traditional news detection methods struggle to keep pace, as fake news often spreads faster and surpasses their capacity. Although these methodologies demonstrate some efficacy against single-modal authentic versus fake content discrimination based on textual data alone, they fall short in addressing real-world scenarios involving multi-source modalities such as integrated text, images, and audio. Furthermore, current approaches lack the flexibility required for emerging categories of misinformation not represented in their training sets—existing models fail to learn features that differentiate fake from genuine news effectively when new sub-types emerge. This paper introduces a cross-modal approach leveraging neural process architecture to identify false news, first establishing emergent false news detection as a new challenge. Specifically, we define the cross-modal fake and real news dataset, presenting a new cross-modal fake news detection task characterized by modal interdependence and heterogeneity in both structure and features. Furthermore, we offer the Meta Neural Process approach which learns a probabilistic link model mapping a source code to a target neural classification head from heterogeneous data across different sources like text, pictures, and audio channels. Specifically designed to detect previously unseen types of fake or real news, the proposed method achieves high accuracy by jointly exploiting multi-source features and leveraging modal dependence and difference. Experimental outcomes highlight significant improvements of our proposed approach using the cross-modal fake and real news dataset compared to existing techniques.

Dynamical models are frequently categorized based on their structural properties, such as linearity or whether they are discrete-time or continuous-time. However, such mathematical classifications may not reflect functional similarities. This paper addresses the problem of clustering differential equation (DE) models that are otherwise undifferentiated, using a new approach called impact-based modeling clustering (IBMC). The primary goal of IBMC is to group models predicted to produce comparable trajectories over a specific domain, even if the resulting outputs differ in scale. To achieve this, we first define a perturbation metric on differential equations and introduce an intrinsic sensitivity index. Subsequently, we apply the Fréchet distance to the resulting perturbation metrics as a clustering criterion. We validate our methodology using two new, public datasets: traditional mathematical examples (e.g., the Lorenz attractor) and biologically significant systems (e.g., gene regulatory networks), demonstrating that we have established the IMBC approach for researchers in fields ranging from physics to biology.

Within the dynamic vocabulary context, the generator produces real texts by assigning vocabulary dimensions dynamically; it achieves a lower divergence from true data distributions by integrating a sparse constraint into the loss function. Complementing this, the loss function for the discriminator explicitly accounts for the difficulty of distinguishing real samples from generated ones. Evaluations using the LinkedIn job posting dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms competing methods in generating text with greater realism and vocabulary diversity while effectively reducing generation costs through the application of sparse coding.

Subsequently, the approach was implemented in particle-resolved large-scale simulations (PR-LSMS) to analyze a 3D silo discharge event, offering the advantage of reduced total computation time compared to standard methods while accurately recapitulating real-time durations. This work examines Ricci shrinkers, a class of shrinking Riemannian metrics that evolve under the reverse Ricci flow. We establish a Liouville theorem demonstrating that any complete Ricci shrinker exhibiting a constant scalar curvature must necessarily be a Yamabe soliton with constant affine parameters under the Ricci flow. Diverging from standard approaches, our proof does not rely on the Bakry - Lebeau operator method. Instead, for non-constant metrics, we define an auxiliary vector field to represent the "translation" and "rotation" components respectively. Subsequently, by analyzing various scenarios, we prove that both affine translation and rotation displacements must vanish when defined over a complete manifold. The secondary part of this paper applies this newly proven theorem to identify necessary conditions for a complete noncompact Ricci shrinker possessing constant scalar curvature.

Recently, Liu et al. However, because this attack causes legitimate inputs to activate poison feature maps with high confidence, it introduces excessive leakage that compromises both model utility and security.

In response, we introduce Dynamic Global Pooling to mitigate the risks inherent in GMP backdoors without necessitating access to a trained model or retraining. Our method partitions a GMP layer associated with a backdoor into multiple small global pools and replaces the standard aggregation method with a dynamic mechanism—such as global average pooling—that selects the channel-wise maximum activation among these regions. This approach effectively suppresses the aggressive activation of poison feature maps caused by existing backdoors while maintaining high-utility outputs and significantly reducing activations of clean-boundary cases compared to direct GMP. Additionally, due to the drastic shrinkage of pool sizes, our strategy offers a much tighter security guarantee against global mean pooling backdoors compared to the original scheme. Recent analyses have drawn attention to how $\gamma$ uncertainty influences astrometric measurements, a factor now critical as missions like Gaia reach their saturation limits in parallax precision. While the remaining parameters have largely minimized traditional parallax errors to sub-all-sky saturation levels, the specific uncertainty in $\gamma$ continues to be a dominant error source. Furthermore, because the estimated value of $\gamma$ fluctuates depending on the specific dataset analyzed, this uncertainty introduces a correlation between individual star measurements and the global $\gamma$ estimate. This study re-examines how $\gamma$ uncertainty impacts parallax precision using a maximum likelihood estimator, employing a statistical random sampling methodology. By decoupling the parameter estimation from the specific dataset used, this mass samples approach eliminates the induced correlations, effectively rendering parallax measurements across the sample independent of one another and of the global estimator.

This study investigates an end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) approach to address language transfer challenges between related languages that share overlapping vocabularies and acoustic patterns. The proposed Model with Hierarchy (MH) integrates a layout designed for progressive refinement. This design operates on an initial stage providing broad equivalence through cross-language AS capabilities, followed by a refined phase leveraging translational equivalence. An AS model was constructed to integrate these components, demonstrating a significant reduction in language-transfer error compared to standard transfer models that utilize independent initializations and those using a language-equivalence mechanism. Results from an English to French AS experiment using 50-hour English and French AS datasets confirm the effectiveness of this method.

We introduce a Temporal Difference learning approach designed to translate an initially ineffective agent, one lacking prior knowledge of a specific environment, into an optimal guide for marine robots navigating similar future, unknown settings. This achievement is realized through Gaussian Process Temporal Difference learning, enhanced by a Bayesian marginal particle inference method tuned via our developed bandwidth selection technique. To validate this approach, experiments were conducted in simulated marine settings, comparing the proposed algorithm against standard Gaussian Process Temporal Difference learning and a random policy baseline, demonstrating significant improvements in real-world applicability for these guides.

We use a generic, monotonic equilibrium fluid interface to examine one-dimensional stellar objects composed of two anisotropic fluids under General Relativity. We present explicit equilibrium conditions with sufficient clarity to facilitate numerical implementation. Our relativistic framework extends earlier work by treating both fluid components as potentially anisotropic. Our simulations demonstrate that multiple equilibrium configurations can exist for specific external parameters; in these cases, stable stellar states comply with the adiabatic theorem, whereas unstable states violate it. Additionally, non-adiabatic equilibria allow us to achieve higher total masses and radii compared to stellar objects constrained to isotropic or single-fluid models.

Automated grammatical error correction (GEC) systems excel at reaching state-of-the-art results when trained on large datasets; however, applying them to new, unrelated domains with only limited data remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a few-shot domain transfer framework for GEC that utilizes only a handful of target-domain examples. We achieve this by adopting a meta-learning approach where the training phase employs diverse GEC tasks across multiple domains to develop an effective parameter update strategy. Consequently, during inference with limited data from a new domain, this method can rapidly adapt to it. Experiments conducted across six different languages and domains demonstrate that even with just 100 or 500 target-domain entries, the proposed method significantly outperforms both traditional full-data GEC models and other existing few-shot techniques.

This paper examines the allocation of indivisible goods among strategic agents with additive valuation functions, operating within an expanded pure Nash equilibrium (PNE) framework where agents can object to both assignments and specific rule implementations. We introduce and analyze a compatibility standard for sharing rule-based mechanisms that guarantee the existence of PNE outcomes. Specifically, we demonstrate that for arbitrary valuations, allocations produced by the generalized round-robin (GRR) rule satisfy this condition endogenous to the mechanism itself. In contrast, we establish that commonly used fixed priority rules and trail-and-turn take-and-make (TTaM) rules fail to meet compatibility within this setting. Nevertheless, we prove that a modified version of TTaM—applied dynamically according to current allocation states rather than an initial fixed sequence—does guarantee PNE existence. Finally, regarding fairness characteristics of PNE allocations, we show that valuation functions that are both convex and concave yield restrictions under which resulting equilibria must violate these properties, respectively.

Although orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) provides excellent resistance to narrowband interference, its inherent wide bandwidth attracts more random perturbations, which can cause information leakage. To enhance security in OFDM systems against eavesdropping, existing methods usually divide the signal into multiple subcarriers; however, allocating transmit power and optimization metrics like secret rate and key generation rates across these carriers often complicates the process significantly. In this paper, the authors address a power-allocation difficulty in AF relay-helped OFDM links by comparing two transmission schemes: independent subcarrier use (where data on each subcarrier is modulated and sent separately) and multi-carrier use (where OFDM signaling is modulated, sent through the channel, and then split after passing through an AF relay). The study evaluates both approaches in terms of bit error rate (BER) performance and physical layer security, ultimately demonstrating that pre-modulation transmission via OFDM—where independent optimization cannot be easily applied—outperforms the method where each subcarrier is optimized independently.

Text-based games function as textual interfaces through which agents navigate virtual environments, execute actions, and receive narrative feedback reflecting the agents' progress. Notably, we demonstrate that agents trained on the earlier TextWorldExpress can operate approximately a thousand times faster than those in the original TextWorld setting, increasing simulation capacity from 1,000 to one million transitions per second.

Physical interactions in cities are known to fluctuate in response to demographic shifts, changes in activity patterns, and pandemic-related measures, yet their specific contributions remain unclear. Utilizing a high-precision tracking dataset of 333,000 individuals across 3.3 million unique urban locations, we distinguish between changes driven by pandemic behaviors and those resulting from urban density variations. Our analysis reveals that during the peak pandemic, the number of urban locations per person fell by 63%. Furthermore, we observe that the resulting decline in urban contact diversity was not equal; non-European participants experienced 2 to 4 fewer varied encounters per person, and men encountered 1.5 times fewer diverse activities than women. Consequently, many communities may face challenges in equitably recovering from post-pandemic rebounds.

Visual noise within an image refers to any flawed content that violates user expectations, ranging from watermarks and compression artifacts to cut-off objects and clipping planes. We further define a new evaluation metric, **ImageSound**, which effectively captures human intuition regarding imagery quality (contrasting with traditional metrics like PSNR or SSIM). LVCNet utilizes an attention mechanism to quantify image noise; remarkably, it reaches an ImageSound score of 96.5% with only 0.1% of the parameters required for PSNR. We demonstrate strong performance through qualitative and quantitative analyses, including real-world applications and robustness to various neural network architectures.
